world.setting: Contemporary American office life: open-plan desks, a manager and a team, a field trip, a bowling-alley team building outing, a basketball arena. Everyday people, no period props.
world.register: contemporary business parable, explanatory, concrete everyday scenes, one idea per beat

young.name: The young employee
young.role: protagonist, searching for a truly effective boss
young.look: A young man in his mid-twenties with short tousled brown hair, a plain navy button-down shirt and khakis, carrying a worn backpack.

manager.name: The manager
manager.role: the one-minute manager who uses short goals, praise and redirects
manager.look: A calm man in his fifties with short gray hair and rimless glasses, wearing a navy suit with a white shirt and a thin tie, always holding a single sheet of paper.

teresa.name: Teresa Lee
teresa.role: field operations manager who learns to own problems
teresa.look: A woman in her forties with shoulder-length dark brown hair tied back, wearing a gray blazer over a blue blouse, carrying one printed page.

paul.name: Paul Trenel
paul.role: employee who presents a client deck and gets specific praise
paul.look: A man in his thirties with a short beard, a light gray sweater and dark trousers, with a laptop bag over one shoulder.

john.name: John Levy
john.role: experienced engineer who makes a costly mistake and is redirected
john.look: A man in his thirties with short dark hair and wire-rim glasses, wearing a navy hoodie over a gray T-shirt with jeans.

office.look: Open-plan office with rows of desks, one manager desk with a single sheet of paper on it, a clock on the wall.

bowling.look: A bowling lane with a canvas bed sheet strung across it, hiding the pins at the far end.

field.look: A plant or field site with a truck and a warning sign, where a problem is spotted.

arena.look: A crowded basketball arena with a bench at the sideline and the scoreboard glowing.

workstation.look: A desk with a laptop and an open slide deck on the screen, a client meeting prepared.

objects.why: The one-page goal: the target everyone can see, agreed side by side.
The bowling game played blind behind a sheet, then played with the sheet lifted.
The one-minute redirect: a sharp, immediate correction that stops at the act.
The one-minute praise: specific recognition given right after the act.
Separating the behavior from the person: the mirror holds up the standard, not the employee.
Self-management: the employee checks their own work against the goal.
The win that comes when the team sees the results clearly.
The one-minute timing: how long each intervention takes.

spine.claim: A busy manager does not need hours of micromanagement; a bowling team blindfolded behind a sheet is the default office, and the fix is one minute at a time.
A young employee searches for a good boss and meets a manager whose one-page goal makes success visible, shared and agreed side by side.
Specific praise given right after the act, with a pause, builds the behavior; a redirect corrects one act, then reaffirms the person.
Management by leaving people alone and zapping them, or by gunny-sacking grievances and being nice before tough, leaves people hiding mistakes and resenting the boss.
The best minute a manager spends is the one invested in people, handing back a sheet and watching the team win on their own.
